rows.stem: Foetal ejection reflex in human female triggers the release of which hormone ?
rows.solution: At the end of pregnancy, signals from the fully developed foetus and the placenta induce mild uterine contractions called the **foetal ejection reflex**. This reflex triggers the release of **oxytocin from the maternal pituitary**. Oxytocin acts on the uterine muscle and causes stronger contractions, which in turn stimulate further secretion of oxytocin, so the cycle continues and leads to expulsion of the baby (parturition). So the answer is option (D) Oxytocin from maternal pituitary gland.

rows.stem: Which of the following is not a functional unit of an ecosystem ?
rows.solution: The functional aspects of an ecosystem are **productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling**. Stratification, the vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels (trees on top, then shrubs, then herbs and grasses), describes the **structure** of an ecosystem, not a function. So the answer is option (C) Stratification.

rows.stem:
Match Column I with Column II and select the correct option :
| Column I | Column II |
|---|---|
| a. Primers | i. \(\beta\)-galactosidase |
| b. Insertional inactivation | ii. To separate and purify products |
| c. Bioreactor | iii. Chemically synthesized oligonucleotides |
| d. Downstream processing | iv. Large scale production of specific product of activity of microbes |
rows.solution:
- a. Primers are small, chemically synthesised oligonucleotides that are complementary to the regions of DNA to be amplified in PCR: a-iii.
- b. Insertional inactivation: a recombinant DNA is inserted within the coding sequence of the enzyme \(\beta\)-galactosidase, which inactivates it, so recombinant colonies give no blue colour with a chromogenic substrate: b-i.
- c. A bioreactor is a large vessel in which raw materials are biologically converted into specific products, so it allows large scale production of a specific product of the activity of microbes: c-iv.
- d. Downstream processing is the separation and purification of the product before it is ready for marketing: d-ii.

So the answer is option (A) a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.

rows.stem: Golden rice is a promising transgenic crop. When released for cultivation, it will help in :

options.label: B
options.text: Reduction of Vitamin A deficiency in humans

rows.solution: Golden rice is a transgenic rice enriched with Vitamin A (\(\beta\)-carotene, the precursor of Vitamin A). Genetic modification has been used to enhance the nutritional value of foods, and Vitamin A enriched rice is the standard example; it can help people whose staple diet is rice and who suffer from Vitamin A deficiency (which causes night blindness). So the answer is option (B) Reduction of Vitamin A deficiency in humans.

rows.stem: Four different transcription units are shown below. Choose the option with the correct image.

options.label: A
options.text: Terminator box at left, Promoter box at right; top strand 3' (left) to 5' (right), TACGACTACGCT, labelled Template strand; bottom strand 5' (left) to 3' (right), ATGCTGATGCGA, labelled Coding strand

options.label: B
options.text: Promoter box at left, Terminator box at right; top strand 5' (left) to 3' (right), TACGACTACGCT, labelled Template strand; bottom strand 3' (left) to 5' (right), ATGCTGATGCGA, labelled Coding strand

options.label: C
options.text: Promoter box at left, Terminator box at right; top strand 3' (left) to 5' (right), TACGACTACGCT, labelled Template strand; bottom strand 5' (left) to 3' (right), ATGCTGATGCGA, labelled Coding strand

options.label: D
options.text: Promoter box at left, Terminator box at right; top strand 3' (left) to 5' (right), TACGACTACGCT, labelled Coding strand; bottom strand 5' (left) to 3' (right), ATGCTGATGCGA, labelled Template strand

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: the four options ARE drawings. Each is a short double-stranded DNA stretch with 'Structural gene' printed above it, a tall box at each end labelled Promoter or Terminator, the 5' and 3' ends of each strand marked with an arrowhead at one end, the same two base sequences, and one strand labelled Template strand and the other Coding strand. The option texts above are a neutral left-to-right reading of each panel (box labels, strand polarities, sequences and strand labels); they name no rule, so the student still has to know that the promoter sits at the 5' end of the coding strand. The drawn originals should be attached. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
In a transcription unit the two strands have opposite polarity. The strand with polarity 3' to 5' acts as the **template strand**; the other strand, 5' to 3', has the same sequence as the RNA (with thymine in place of uracil) and is the **coding strand**. The **promoter** lies towards the **5' end (upstream) of the structural gene**, with reference to the polarity of the coding strand, and the **terminator** lies towards its **3' end (downstream)**.

Checking the drawings against these rules:
- The drawing with the promoter at the left, the template strand on top running 3' to 5' and the coding strand below running 5' to 3' satisfies all of them: the promoter sits at the 5' end of the coding strand and the terminator at its 3' end. The coding strand also begins with ATG, the start codon.
- The drawing with the promoter on the right places it at the 3' end of the coding strand, which is where the terminator belongs.
- The drawing whose bottom (coding) strand runs 3' to 5' from the promoter end places the promoter at the 3' end of the coding strand, and its template strand runs 5' to 3'.
- The drawing in which the 3' to 5' strand is labelled coding strand and the 5' to 3' strand template strand has the two labels the wrong way round, so its promoter again sits at the 3' end of the coding strand.

So the answer is option (C), the drawing with the promoter box at the left, the template strand running 3' to 5' on top and the coding strand running 5' to 3' below.

rows.stem: Appearance of antibiotic-resistant bacteria is an example of evolution due to :
rows.solution: Excessive use of antibiotics kills the sensitive microbes, and the few resistant ones survive and multiply, so in a few years a resistant population appears. Similarly, excess use of herbicides and pesticides has selected resistant varieties in a much shorter time scale. Because the selecting agent is a human activity, this is called **evolution by anthropogenic action**. So the answer is option (D) Anthropogenic action.

rows.stem:
Identify the statements that correctly describe Darwin's Theory of Evolution.
(i) Overproduction of organisms leads to competition.
(ii) Variation is inherited and causes evolution.
(iii) Acquired characters are inherited.
(iv) Survival depends on favourable traits.
(v) New species arise due to accumulation of favourable variations.
Choose the correct option.
rows.solution:
Darwin's theory of natural selection rests on these points:
- (i) is correct: organisms produce more offspring than can survive, and the overproduction leads to a struggle for existence (competition).
- (ii) is correct: heritable variations exist, and it is these inherited variations that make evolution possible.
- (iii) is wrong: the inheritance of acquired characters (use and disuse) was proposed by **Lamarck**, not Darwin.
- (iv) is correct: individuals with favourable variations are better fit, survive and leave more progeny (survival of the fittest).
- (v) is correct: favourable variations accumulate over generations and, in the course of time, give rise to new species.

So the answer is option (A) (i), (ii), (iv) and (v) are correct.

rows.stem: Which of the following is not a symptom of Ascariasis ?
rows.solution: Ascariasis is caused by the intestinal parasite Ascaris, the common roundworm. Its symptoms include **internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia and blockage of the intestinal passage**. Skin ulcers are not a symptom of ascariasis. So the answer is option (D) Skin ulcers.

rows.stem: Every trophic level has a certain mass of living material at a particular time. What is it called ?
rows.solution: Each trophic level has a certain mass of living material at a particular time, called the **standing crop**. It is measured as the biomass of living organisms or as their number in a unit area. (The standing state is the amount of inorganic nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus present in the soil at a given time, and primary productivity is a rate of biomass production, not a mass present at one time.) So the answer is option (A) Standing crop.

rows.stem: The smallest part of DNA molecule that can be changed by point mutation is :
rows.solution: A point mutation arises from a change in a **single base pair** of DNA, for example the substitution that causes sickle-cell anaemia. A base pair is made of nucleotides, so the smallest part of a DNA molecule that a point mutation can change is a **nucleotide**; a codon (three nucleotides) or a whole gene is changed only as a consequence. So the answer is option (D) Nucleotide.

rows.stem:
Some statements regarding drugs and alcohol are given below :
(i) Adolescents are more vulnerable to peer pressure.
(ii) Drug addiction leads to increased tolerance level of the receptors present in our body.
(iii) Alcohol affects the central nervous system.
(iv) Excessive use of drugs helps to increase energy.
(v) Anabolic steroids decrease aggressiveness.
Choose the option with correct statement(s).
rows.solution:
- (i) is correct: adolescents are vulnerable and often take drugs or alcohol because of peer pressure and curiosity.
- (ii) is correct: repeated use of drugs increases the **tolerance level of the receptors** present in our body, so the receptors respond only to higher doses, which leads to addiction.
- (iii) is correct: alcohol affects the central nervous system (and chronic use damages the liver as well).
- (iv) is wrong: excessive use of drugs does not increase energy; it harms the nervous system, liver and other organs.
- (v) is wrong: anabolic steroids **increase** aggressiveness and cause mood swings.

So the answer is option (B) Statements (i), (ii) and (iii) are correct.

rows.stem: Select the correct option for the pair of plants pollinated by water.
rows.solution: Pollination by water is quite rare and is limited to about 30 genera, mostly monocotyledons. Examples are Vallisneria and Hydrilla, which grow in fresh water, and marine sea-grasses such as Zostera. In most aquatic plants such as water hyacinth and water lily the flowers emerge above the water and are pollinated by insects or wind, and Parthenium is a land weed. So the pair pollinated by water is Vallisneria and Hydrilla. So the answer is option (A) Vallisneria and Hydrilla.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Activated sludge contains large population of bacteria.
Reason (R) : These bacteria help in anaerobic digestion of human waste in biogas plant.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: in secondary treatment, the bacterial flocs settle in the settling tank and this sediment, the **activated sludge**, contains a large population of bacteria; a small part of it is pumped back into the aeration tank as inoculum. The Reason is false: the flocs are made of **aerobic** bacteria that digest organic matter in the aeration tank. The major part of the sludge is pumped into large tanks called **anaerobic sludge digesters**, where other kinds of bacteria, which grow anaerobically, digest the bacteria and fungi in the sludge and produce biogas. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Ecosystems require a constant supply of energy to synthesize the molecules they require.
Reason (R) : This is to counteract the universal tendency towards increasing disorderliness as per Second Law of Thermodynamics.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: all organisms, and so all ecosystems, need a constant input of energy (mainly sunlight fixed by producers) to synthesise the molecules they require. The Reason is true and explains it: ecosystems are not exempt from the **Second Law of Thermodynamics**, so without a continuous supply of energy their ordered molecules would drift towards increasing disorderliness. So both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : DNA cannot pass through cell membrane of a bacterial cell.
Reason (R) : DNA is a hydrophilic molecule.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: DNA cannot pass through the cell membrane of a bacterium on its own, which is why the cell has to be made **competent** (for example by treatment with a divalent cation such as calcium, followed by a heat shock) before it can take up recombinant DNA. The Reason is true and explains it: DNA is a **hydrophilic** molecule, and a hydrophilic molecule cannot pass through the lipid layers of a cell membrane. So both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Repetitive sequences are stretches of DNA sequences that are thought to have no direct coding functions.
Reason (R) : They shed light on chromosome structure, dynamics and evolution.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Both statements come from the salient features of the human genome. The Assertion is true: repetitive sequences are stretches of DNA sequences repeated many times, sometimes hundreds to thousands of times, and they are thought to have no direct coding functions. The Reason is also true: they shed light on chromosome structure, dynamics and evolution. But the Reason does not explain the Assertion: what the sequences reveal to us is not why they lack a coding function. So both statements are true but the Reason does not explain the Assertion, which is option (B).

rows.stem:
A person complains of persistent itching in the groin region and scalp. The person also shows dry and scaly lesions on skin, nails, etc.
(i) Identify the disease.
(ii) Name its two causative agents.
(iii) Mention its mode of transmission.
rows.solution:
(i) The disease is **ringworm**, a common fungal infection; dry, scaly lesions on the skin, nails and scalp accompanied by intense itching are its main symptoms. Heat and moisture help the fungi grow, which is why it appears in skin folds such as the groin.

(ii) Ringworm is caused by fungi of the genera **Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton** (any two).

(iii) It is generally acquired **from the soil or by using the towels, clothes or even the comb of an infected individual**.

rows.stem:
A girl develops sneezing, watery eyes and difficulty in breathing every time she visits a flower garden.
(i) Identify the condition.
(ii) Name the immune component responsible for this condition.
(iii) Name the chemical released.
(iv) State one medicine used to treat such a condition.
rows.solution:
(i) The condition is an **allergy**, an exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens (allergens) present in the environment, here pollen in the flower garden.

(ii) The antibodies produced in response to allergens are of the **IgE** type.

(iii) Allergy is due to the release of chemicals such as **histamine and serotonin** from the mast cells (any one).

(iv) The symptoms can be quickly reduced by drugs such as **anti-histamines, adrenalin or steroids** (any one).

rows.stem:
(i) Mention any two characteristics of Neanderthal man that lived near East and Central Asia.
(ii) Identify the following hominids with respect to human evolution :
(I) Brain capacity 900 cc, probably ate meat.
(II) First human-like with brain capacity 650 – 800 cc.
rows.solution:
(i) Characteristics of the Neanderthal man, who lived in the near east and central Asian countries (any two):
- a **brain size of about 1400 cc**;
- they **used hides to protect their bodies**;
- they **buried their dead**.

(ii)
- (I) A brain capacity of about 900 cc, and probably ate meat: **Homo erectus**.
- (II) The first human-like being, with a brain capacity of 650 to 800 cc: **Homo habilis** (who probably did not eat meat).

rows.stem:
The allele for brown eyes (B) is dominant over blue eyes (b). In a population, 36% of individuals have blue eyes.
Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, calculate :
(i) Frequency of allele B
(ii) Percentage of heterozygous individuals
(iii) Percentage of individuals that are homozygous dominant
(Working to be shown)
rows.solution:
Let \(p\) be the frequency of the dominant allele B and \(q\) that of the recessive allele b. Blue-eyed individuals are homozygous recessive (bb), so their frequency is \(q^2\).

(i) \(q^2 = 36\% = 0.36\), so \(q = \sqrt{0.36} = 0.6\).
Since \(p + q = 1\), \(p = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4\). The frequency of allele B is **0.4**.

(ii) Heterozygous individuals (Bb) have frequency \(2pq = 2 \times 0.4 \times 0.6 = 0.48\), that is **48%**.

(iii) Homozygous dominant individuals (BB) have frequency \(p^2 = 0.4 \times 0.4 = 0.16\), that is **16%**.

Check: \(p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 0.16 + 0.48 + 0.36 = 1\).

rows.stem: What did Henking observe in his experiments on insects that led to the discovery of sex chromosome ? How did his observation contribute to our understanding of sex determination ?
rows.solution:
In 1891, Henking traced a specific nuclear structure all through spermatogenesis in a few insects. He observed that **50 per cent of the sperms received this structure after spermatogenesis, whereas the other 50 per cent did not**. He named it the X body, but could not explain its significance; later investigators showed that it was in fact a chromosome, and it was named the **X-chromosome**.

This observation laid the basis of chromosomal sex determination. In such insects (the XO type, for example the grasshopper), all eggs carry one X chromosome, while the sperms are of two kinds:
- eggs fertilised by a sperm carrying the X chromosome develop into **females**;
- eggs fertilised by a sperm without the X chromosome develop into **males**.

So the sex of the offspring is decided by the kind of sperm that fertilises the egg.

rows.stem:
(i) Given below is the schematic representation of the process of electrophoresis. Identify the alphabets representing the :
(I) Anode end, and
(II) Lightest/Smallest DNA in matrix.
(ii) What is Agarose gel and why is it used in this process ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a rectangular gel with four lanes numbered 1 to 4, a box in each lane, and bars of DNA bands along each lane; its two ends are labelled 'end U' and 'end S', and circled letters P, Q and R point into the gel from above and T from below. Where the wells sit, which way the bands have spread and what each of P, Q, R and T points at decide both parts of (i), so they are withheld here. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
(i) DNA fragments are negatively charged, so in an electric field they move from the wells at one end towards the **anode**, the positive electrode, at the other end. The bands have spread away from the wells towards end S, so:
- (I) the anode end is **S**;
- (II) the smaller the fragment, the farther it moves through the gel, so the lightest or smallest DNA is the band that has travelled farthest from the wells towards the anode, the band marked **R**.

(ii) **Agarose** is a natural polymer extracted from sea weeds. It is used as the matrix in gel electrophoresis because it provides a **sieving effect**: the DNA fragments separate (resolve) according to their size, smaller fragments moving farther than larger ones.

rows.stem:
After performing gel electrophoresis, a student observes that DNA fragments are not visible.
(i) Suggest a reason for this and explain how fragments can be made visible.
(ii) Also explain how a specific DNA fragment can be collected from the gel for further use.
rows.solution:
(i) The DNA fragments are not visible because they have not been **stained with ethidium bromide and exposed to UV radiation**: pure DNA fragments cannot be seen in visible light. After staining with ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation, the fragments are seen as **bright orange coloured bands**.

(ii) The band containing the desired DNA fragment is **cut out from the agarose gel** and the DNA is extracted from the gel piece. This step is known as **elution**. The purified fragment can then be used to construct recombinant DNA by joining it with a cloning vector.

rows.stem:
GEAC is a regulatory body under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in India.
(a) Write the full form of GEAC.
(b) Mention two of its important functions related to biotechnology.
rows.solution:
(a) GEAC stands for **Genetic Engineering Approval Committee**.

(b) Its important functions related to biotechnology:
- it makes decisions regarding the **validity of GM (genetic modification) research**;
- it decides on the **safety of introducing genetically modified organisms for public services**.

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(a) Explain the different ways by which apomictic seeds can be developed.
(b) Mention one advantage of apomictic seeds for farmers.
rows.solution:
(a) Apomixis is the production of seeds without fertilisation, and it happens in two ways:
- In some species, such as many members of Asteraceae and grasses, the **diploid egg cell is formed without reduction division** and develops into an embryo **without fertilisation**.
- More often, as in many Citrus and mango varieties, some of the **nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos**. Such seeds may contain several embryos (polyembryony).

(b) Hybrid seeds have to be produced every year, because if the seeds collected from hybrids are sown, the plants in the progeny segregate and do not keep the hybrid characters. If the hybrids are made into apomicts, there is **no segregation of characters in the hybrid progeny**, so farmers can keep using the hybrid seeds to raise new crops year after year instead of buying them every year, which makes them cost effective.

rows.stem:
(a) What is meant by translation in protein synthesis ?
(b) Explain charging of tRNA (aminoacylation of tRNA) and mention its importance in the process of translation.
rows.solution:
(a) **Translation** is the process of **polymerisation of amino acids to form a polypeptide**. The order and sequence of the amino acids are defined by the sequence of bases in the mRNA, and the amino acids are joined by peptide bonds.

(b) Forming a peptide bond requires energy. So, in the first phase, the amino acids are **activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA**. This process is called **charging of tRNA**, or aminoacylation of tRNA.

Its importance: if two such charged tRNAs are brought close enough, the **formation of a peptide bond between their amino acids is favoured energetically**. The charged tRNA also carries its amino acid to the ribosome and matches it to the right codon on the mRNA through its anticodon.

rows.stem:
(a) What is the carrying capacity of a species in a habitat ?
(b) Explain the growth curve that takes this capacity into account.
rows.solution:
(a) The **carrying capacity (K)** is the limit to the maximum number of individuals of a species (the population size) that a habitat can support with its available resources, beyond which no further growth is possible.

(b) The growth curve that takes the carrying capacity into account is the **Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth** model. No population can grow exponentially for long, because resources become limiting and the individuals compete for them. A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows:
- an initial **lag phase**,
- followed by phases of **acceleration** and **deceleration**,
- and finally an **asymptote**, when the population density reaches the carrying capacity.

A plot of population density (N) against time (t) is therefore a **sigmoid (S-shaped) curve**, described by \(\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\frac{K - N}{K}\right)\), where N is the population density at time t, r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase and K is the carrying capacity. The curve is drawn with N on the vertical axis and t on the horizontal, labelled with the lag phase, the asymptote and K as a dashed line that the curve levels off against.

rows.stem:
In vitro fertilization (IVF) is a popular method these days that is helping childless couples to bear a child.
(a) Write the different steps that are carried out in this technique.
(b) Would you consider gamete intra fallopian transfer as a type of IVF ? Justify your answer.
rows.solution:
(a) In vitro fertilisation (IVF) is fertilisation outside the body, in almost similar conditions as in the body, followed by embryo transfer (popularly, a test tube baby). Its steps:
- **Ova from the wife or a donor female and sperms from the husband or a donor male are collected** and induced to form a zygote under simulated conditions in the laboratory.
- The zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the **fallopian tube (ZIFT, zygote intra fallopian transfer)**,
- while an embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the **uterus (IUT, intra uterine transfer)**, to complete its further development.

(b) **No.** In IVF the fertilisation takes place in the laboratory, outside the female body. In GIFT (gamete intra fallopian transfer) an ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of another female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and further development, so the **fertilisation takes place inside the female's body** (in vivo). GIFT is therefore not a type of IVF.

rows.stem: Draw a neat diagram of a maize grain showing the internal structure and label any five parts.
rows.solution:
The diagram is a longitudinal section of a maize grain, oval in outline, labelled as follows (any five labels, plus the diagram):
- **Pericarp**: the thin outer covering; in a grain the seed coat is fused with it.
- **Endosperm**: the large, food-storing region filling most of the grain, at the top and one side.
- **Aleurone layer**: the proteinaceous outermost layer of the endosperm, just inside the pericarp.
- **Scutellum**: the large, shield-shaped single cotyledon, lying against the endosperm.
- **Coleoptile**: the hollow foliar sheath enclosing the shoot apex.
- **Plumule** (shoot apex with a few leaf primordia), inside the coleoptile.
- **Radicle** (root cap and root tip), at the lower end of the embryonal axis.
- **Coleorhiza**: the undifferentiated sheath enclosing the radicle.

The embryo lies on one side of the grain, against the endosperm, with the scutellum towards the endosperm and the plumule pointing upwards and the radicle downwards.

rows.stem:
Cow dung and water are mixed and fed into a biogas plant to allow digestion of biowastes. The person performing this process says that there is no need to provide an inoculum.
(a) Do you agree with him ? Justify your answer.
(b) What happens to the biowaste inside the digester ?
(c) Name the useful by-products obtained from this process and mention how they are used.
rows.solution:
(a) **Yes**, he is right. Cow dung (gobar) is rich in **methanogenic bacteria** such as Methanobacterium, which are also present in the rumen of cattle. So the dung itself provides the microbes that digest the biowaste, and no separate inoculum is needed.

(b) Inside the airtight digester the biowaste is **digested by anaerobic bacteria, the methanogens present in the cow dung**. They grow anaerobically on the cellulosic material and produce large amounts of **methane** along with carbon dioxide and hydrogen. This gas mixture is biogas.

(c) Useful by-products and their uses:
- **Biogas**, which is used for **cooking and lighting**;
- the **spent slurry**, which is removed through an outlet and used as **fertiliser (manure)**.

rows.stem:
(a) Describe the experiment conducted by T.H. Morgan on Drosophila melanogaster involving eye colour and body colour.
(b) How did the results deviate from Mendelian inheritance pattern ?
(c) Explain the two genetic terms used by Morgan for his observations.
rows.solution:
(a) T.H. Morgan carried out several dihybrid crosses in Drosophila to study sex-linked genes. In one, he hybridised **yellow-bodied, white-eyed females with brown-bodied, red-eyed males** and intercrossed their \(\text{F}_1\) progeny. Both genes, for body colour and eye colour, are located on the X chromosome.

(b) He observed that **the two genes did not segregate independently of each other**, so the \(\text{F}_2\) ratio **deviated very significantly from the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio** expected when two genes assort independently. The parental gene combinations appeared much more often than the non-parental ones.

(c) The two terms Morgan used:
- **Linkage**: the physical association of genes on a chromosome. When genes are grouped on the same chromosome, some are very tightly linked and show very low recombination, as with the genes for white eye and yellow body (1.3 per cent), while others are loosely linked and show higher recombination (37.2 per cent for white eye and miniature wing).
- **Recombination**: the generation of non-parental gene combinations.

rows.stem: With reference to the above graph, explain the concentration of nicotine in the blood at 10 minutes.
rows.context: The data below shows the concentration of nicotine smoked by a smoker taking 10 puffs/minute.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a line graph titled 'Smoking Cigarette', Concentration of Nicotine in blood (mg per cubic cm, 0 to 50 in steps of 5) against Time (minutes, 1 to 15), drawn as one connected line. The value the line reaches at 10 minutes, and how it compares with the rest of the curve, is exactly what (a)(i) asks, so the line's course is withheld here. Page idx 20.
rows.solution: The graph shows the nicotine concentration in the blood rising steadily while the smoker takes 10 puffs a minute, because nicotine is absorbed through the lungs into the blood faster than it is removed. At **10 minutes it reaches its maximum, about 45 mg per \(\text{cm}^3\)**; after that the concentration falls sharply, showing that smoking has stopped and the nicotine is being removed from the blood.

rows.stem: How will this affect the concentration of carbon monoxide and haem-bound oxygen at 10 minutes ?
rows.context: The data below shows the concentration of nicotine smoked by a smoker taking 10 puffs/minute.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: the case study's 'Smoking Cigarette' line graph of nicotine concentration in blood against time; 'this' refers to the nicotine level the graph shows at 10 minutes, so the line's course is withheld here. Page idx 20.
rows.solution: Smoking increases the **carbon monoxide content of the blood**, and carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen. So at 10 minutes, when the intake is greatest, the concentration of carbon monoxide **increases** and the concentration of **haem-bound oxygen decreases**, which causes oxygen deficiency in the body.

rows.stem: How does cigarette smoking result in high blood pressure and increase in heart rate ?
rows.context: The data below shows the concentration of nicotine smoked by a smoker taking 10 puffs/minute.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE: the case study's 'Smoking Cigarette' line graph of nicotine concentration in blood against time, attached so the passage's 'data below' is not left dangling; the question is answerable from text. Page idx 20.
rows.solution: Tobacco smoke contains nicotine, an alkaloid. Nicotine **stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline into the blood circulation**, and both these hormones **raise the blood pressure and increase the heart rate**.

rows.stem: To which class of compounds does nicotine belong ? Name one other drug from the same class.
rows.context: The data below shows the concentration of nicotine smoked by a smoker taking 10 puffs/minute.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE: the case study's 'Smoking Cigarette' line graph of nicotine concentration in blood against time, attached so the passage's 'data below' is not left dangling; the question is answerable from text. Page idx 20.
rows.solution: [CBSE marking scheme: its list of accepted drugs also includes cannabinoids, which are not alkaloids; they are a separate group of chemicals that act on the cannabinoid receptors of the brain. Cocaine and morphine are alkaloids.] Nicotine belongs to the class of **alkaloids**. Another drug from the same class is **cocaine**, the alkaloid obtained from the coca plant (also taken as coke or crack); **morphine**, the opium alkaloid from the poppy plant, is another.

rows.stem: Which method conserves the highest number of species ? Is it ex situ or in situ conservation ?
rows.context:
India is one of the megadiverse countries housing around \(8{\cdot}1\) per cent of global species diversity, although its land area is only \(2{\cdot}4\) per cent of the world's land area. Many of the species are highly threatened due to human activities like deforestation, mining and habitat fragmentation. Laws like Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 were enacted by the Government of India to preserve our biological wealth. Various conservation measures are being implemented to save the threatened species.
The following bar graph shows the number of species conserved under different biodiversity conservation methods.
Study the graph and answer the questions.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a bar graph titled 'Species Conserved under Different Biodiversity Conservation Methods', Number of Species Conserved (0 to 3000) against Conservation Method, five bars each with its count printed above it. The method named under each bar and the counts decide (a), so they are withheld here. Page idx 22.
rows.solution: **Wildlife sanctuaries** conserve the highest number of species, 2500 in the graph. This is **in situ** conservation, because the species are protected in their natural habitat.

rows.stem: Which other methods shown in the diagram are opposite to the one identified by you in question (a) ? How are these two conservation approaches different ?
rows.context:
India is one of the megadiverse countries housing around \(8{\cdot}1\) per cent of global species diversity, although its land area is only \(2{\cdot}4\) per cent of the world's land area. Many of the species are highly threatened due to human activities like deforestation, mining and habitat fragmentation. Laws like Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 were enacted by the Government of India to preserve our biological wealth. Various conservation measures are being implemented to save the threatened species.
The following bar graph shows the number of species conserved under different biodiversity conservation methods.
Study the graph and answer the questions.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: the case study's bar graph of species conserved under five conservation methods; the five methods are named only under the bars, and (b) asks which of them are the opposite approach, so the method names are withheld here. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
**Zoological parks and botanical gardens** are the opposite approach: they are **ex situ** conservation, while wildlife sanctuaries (like national parks and biosphere reserves) are in situ.

How the two approaches differ (any one):

| In situ conservation | Ex situ conservation |
|---|---|
| Organisms are protected in their natural habitat. | Organisms are taken out of their natural habitat and placed in special settings where they can be protected and given special care. |
| The whole ecosystem is conserved, so biodiversity at all levels is protected. | It is used for threatened or endangered animals and plants that need urgent measures to save them from extinction. |

rows.stem: Write two features of Biodiversity hotspots.
rows.context:
India is one of the megadiverse countries housing around \(8{\cdot}1\) per cent of global species diversity, although its land area is only \(2{\cdot}4\) per cent of the world's land area. Many of the species are highly threatened due to human activities like deforestation, mining and habitat fragmentation. Laws like Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 were enacted by the Government of India to preserve our biological wealth. Various conservation measures are being implemented to save the threatened species.
The following bar graph shows the number of species conserved under different biodiversity conservation methods.
Study the graph and answer the questions.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE: the case study's bar graph of species conserved under five conservation methods, attached so the passage's 'following bar graph' is not left dangling; the question is answerable from text. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
Biodiversity hotspots are regions with:
- a **very high level of species richness**, and
- a **high degree of endemism**, that is, many species confined to that region and found nowhere else.

They are also regions where this diversity is seriously threatened by habitat loss.

rows.stem: To which category do sacred groves belong and how do they help in bio-conservation ?
rows.context:
India is one of the megadiverse countries housing around \(8{\cdot}1\) per cent of global species diversity, although its land area is only \(2{\cdot}4\) per cent of the world's land area. Many of the species are highly threatened due to human activities like deforestation, mining and habitat fragmentation. Laws like Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 were enacted by the Government of India to preserve our biological wealth. Various conservation measures are being implemented to save the threatened species.
The following bar graph shows the number of species conserved under different biodiversity conservation methods.
Study the graph and answer the questions.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE: the case study's bar graph of species conserved under five conservation methods, attached so the passage's 'following bar graph' is not left dangling; the question is answerable from text. Page idx 22.
rows.solution: Sacred groves belong to **in situ conservation**. In many cultures, tracts of forest were set aside and **all the trees and wildlife within them were venerated and given total protection**. So the groves act as refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants. Examples are found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh.

rows.stem:
(i) Describe the series of experiments conducted by Frederick Griffith. Comment on the significance of the result obtained.
(ii) State the contribution of Avery, MacLeod and McCarty.
rows.solution:
(i) In 1928, Frederick Griffith worked with the bacterium Streptococcus pneumoniae, which causes pneumonia, using two strains:
- the **S strain (smooth)**, whose cells have a mucous (polysaccharide) coat, which is **virulent**;
- the **R strain (rough)**, which has no coat and is **non-virulent**.

He injected these bacteria into mice in a series of experiments:
- S strain \(\rightarrow\) injected into mice \(\rightarrow\) the mice die.
- R strain \(\rightarrow\) injected into mice \(\rightarrow\) the mice live.
- S strain (heat-killed) \(\rightarrow\) injected into mice \(\rightarrow\) the mice live.
- S strain (heat-killed) + R strain (live) \(\rightarrow\) injected into mice \(\rightarrow\) the mice die.

He also **recovered living S bacteria from the dead mice**.

Significance: the R strain bacteria had somehow been **transformed** by the heat-killed S strain bacteria. Griffith concluded that some "**transforming principle**", transferred from the heat-killed S strain, had enabled the R strain to synthesise a smooth polysaccharide coat and become virulent. This must have been due to the transfer of the genetic material, although his experiments did not show what that material was.

(ii) **Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty** (1933 to 1944) worked to determine the **biochemical nature of the transforming principle** in Griffith's experiment:
- they purified biochemicals (proteins, DNA, RNA and so on) from the heat-killed S cells to see which ones could transform live R cells into S cells;
- they discovered that **DNA alone from the S bacteria caused the R bacteria to become transformed**;
- **protein-digesting enzymes (proteases) and RNA-digesting enzymes (RNases) did not affect transformation**, so the transforming substance was neither a protein nor RNA;
- **digestion with DNase did inhibit transformation**, showing that DNA caused it.

They concluded that **DNA is the hereditary material**.

rows.stem:
The following questions are based on haemophilia.
(i) Work out the crosses between :
(I) Normal female and Haemophilic male
(II) Carrier female and Normal male
(III) Carrier female and Haemophilic male
(ii) Write the conclusions you draw from these crosses. Comment on the type of inheritance of the disease.
(Use : X – Normal, \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\) – Haemophilic)
rows.solution:
(i) Haemophilia is caused by a recessive gene on the X chromosome, written \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\); X is the normal allele.

(I) Normal female (XX) \(\times\) haemophilic male (\(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\text{Y}\)). Gametes: female X, X; male \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\), Y.

| Eggs / Sperms | \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\) | Y |
|---|---|---|
| X | \(\text{XX}^{\text{h}}\) (carrier girl) | XY (normal boy) |
| X | \(\text{XX}^{\text{h}}\) (carrier girl) | XY (normal boy) |

All the daughters are carriers and all the sons are normal.

(II) Carrier female (\(\text{XX}^{\text{h}}\)) \(\times\) normal male (XY). Gametes: female X, \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\); male X, Y.

| Eggs / Sperms | X | Y |
|---|---|---|
| X | XX (normal girl) | XY (normal boy) |
| \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\) | \(\text{XX}^{\text{h}}\) (carrier girl) | \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\text{Y}\) (haemophilic boy) |

Half the daughters are carriers and half the sons are haemophilic.

(III) Carrier female (\(\text{XX}^{\text{h}}\)) \(\times\) haemophilic male (\(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\text{Y}\)). Gametes: female X, \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\); male \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\), Y.

| Eggs / Sperms | \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\) | Y |
|---|---|---|
| X | \(\text{XX}^{\text{h}}\) (carrier girl) | XY (normal boy) |
| \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\) | \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\text{X}^{\text{h}}\) (haemophilic girl) | \(\text{X}^{\text{h}}\text{Y}\) (haemophilic boy) |

Half the daughters are haemophilic and half are carriers; half the sons are haemophilic.

(ii) Conclusions:
- The disease is transmitted from an **unaffected carrier female to some of her male progeny**; a haemophilic father never passes it to his sons, only to his daughters, who become carriers.
- A **haemophilic female is extremely rare**, because her mother has to be at least a carrier and her father has to be haemophilic, and haemophilic males are often unviable in the later stage of life.

Type of inheritance: haemophilia is a **sex-linked (X-linked) recessive disorder**.

rows.stem:
(i) Explain any two basic principles/core techniques on which biotechnology is based.
(ii) Describe any three key tools used in Recombinant DNA technology.
rows.solution:
(i) Among many, the two core techniques that enabled the birth of modern biotechnology are:
- **Genetic engineering**: techniques to alter the chemistry of the genetic material (DNA and RNA), to introduce it into host organisms and thus change the phenotype of the host organism.
- **Bioprocess engineering**: maintenance of a sterile (microbial contamination-free) ambience in chemical engineering processes, to enable the growth of only the desired microbe or eukaryotic cell in large quantities for the manufacture of biotechnological products such as antibiotics, vaccines and enzymes.

(ii) Key tools of recombinant DNA technology (any three):
- **Restriction enzymes** (molecular scissors): they cut DNA at specific points in the sugar-phosphate backbone, recognising specific palindromic nucleotide sequences, and many of them leave **sticky ends** that help join DNA from different sources with the help of DNA ligase.
- **Cloning vectors**: DNA molecules such as plasmids and bacteriophages that can replicate in a host cell and are used to **carry foreign genes into a host cell**; they carry an origin of replication, selectable markers and cloning sites.
- **Competent host**: the living organism (often a bacterium such as E. coli) into which the **recombinant DNA is introduced**. Since DNA is hydrophilic, the host cells are first made competent to take it up, for example by treatment with calcium ions followed by a heat shock.

DNA ligase and DNA polymerase are the other enzymes used as tools.

rows.stem:
"Early and accurate diagnosis of diseases is vital in medical technology."
(i) Name the conventional methods of diagnosis and their disadvantages.
(ii) Which three diagnostic techniques have been developed through Biotechnology ? Explain how each one helps in detecting diseases.
rows.solution:
(i) The conventional methods of diagnosis are **serum and urine analysis** (also stool and sputum analysis). Their disadvantage: they **do not allow early detection**. A pathogen can be detected only when its concentration has become high, that is, when the disease has spread and the symptoms have appeared.

(ii) Biotechnology offers techniques of early diagnosis:
- **PCR (polymerase chain reaction)**: it amplifies a specific nucleic acid sequence, so very low concentrations of a bacterium or virus, present before the symptoms appear, can be detected. It is used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients and mutations in genes of suspected cancer patients.
- **ELISA (enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay)**: it works on the principle of **antigen-antibody interaction**. Infection by a pathogen is detected by the presence of antigens (proteins, glycoproteins and so on) or by detecting the antibodies synthesised against the pathogen.
- **Recombinant DNA probe with autoradiography**: a single-stranded DNA or RNA tagged with a radioactive molecule (a probe) is allowed to hybridise to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells, followed by detection using autoradiography. A clone having a mutated gene will not appear on the photographic film, because the probe will not find complementarity with the mutated gene.

rows.stem:
Oogenesis is a discontinuous process that begins before birth and is completed after puberty.
(i) Trace the development of a gamete mother cell till its release from the ovary during ovulation.
(ii) Name the two pituitary hormones that play an important role in the process.
rows.solution:
(i) The development of a gamete mother cell (oogonium) till ovulation:
- Oogenesis begins during foetal development, when a couple of million **gamete mother cells (oogonia)**, which are diploid, are formed in each foetal ovary by mitosis; no more oogonia are formed or added after birth.
- The oogonia start meiosis I and enter its prophase, where they get **temporarily arrested as primary oocytes**. Each primary oocyte gets surrounded by a layer of granulosa cells and is then called a **primary follicle**. A large number of these follicles degenerate between birth and puberty, so only 60,000 to 80,000 remain in each ovary at puberty.
- The primary follicles get surrounded by more layers of granulosa cells and a new theca, becoming **secondary follicles**. A secondary follicle soon transforms into a **tertiary follicle**, characterised by a fluid-filled cavity called the antrum; its theca organises into an inner theca interna and an outer theca externa.
- The primary oocyte within the tertiary follicle grows in size and **completes meiosis I**, an unequal division giving a large haploid **secondary oocyte** and a tiny **first polar body**. The secondary oocyte keeps the bulk of the nutrient-rich cytoplasm.
- The tertiary follicle changes into the mature **Graafian follicle**, and the secondary oocyte forms a new membrane, the zona pellucida, around it. The secondary oocyte starts meiosis II and stops at that stage.
- The Graafian follicle **ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (ovum) from the ovary**. This is **ovulation**. Meiosis II is completed only when a sperm enters, forming the ovum and a second polar body.

In a diagram: oogonia (fetal life) \(\rightarrow\) mitosis and differentiation \(\rightarrow\) primary oocyte \(\rightarrow\) (birth, childhood, puberty) first meiotic division, completed prior to ovulation \(\rightarrow\) secondary oocyte + first polar body \(\rightarrow\) (adult reproductive life) ovum + second polar body.

(ii) The two pituitary hormones are **FSH (follicle stimulating hormone)**, which stimulates the growth of the ovarian follicles, and **LH (luteinising hormone)**, whose mid-cycle surge induces rupture of the Graafian follicle and so ovulation.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw a labelled two-celled structure of male gametophyte of an angiosperm.
(ii) Name the three layers that surround the cytoplasm of a male gametophyte starting from innermost to outermost layer.
(iii) Which organic material makes the outermost layer ? Mention its advantage.
(iv) Why is the outermost layer of male gametophyte not continuous ?
rows.solution:
(i) The diagram is a round, mature pollen grain (male gametophyte) at the two-celled stage, labelled:
- **Vegetative cell**: the bigger cell, with abundant food reserve and a large, irregularly shaped nucleus;
- **Generative cell**: the small, spindle-shaped cell with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus, floating in the cytoplasm of the vegetative cell;
- the wall, with the outer **exine** and its **germ pore**, and the inner **intine**.

(ii) Starting from the innermost layer: **plasma membrane**, then **intine**, then **exine**.

(iii) The exine is made of **sporopollenin**, one of the most resistant organic materials known. It can **withstand high temperatures and strong acids and alkali, and no enzyme that degrades sporopollenin is so far known**. This protects the pollen grain, and it is why pollen grains are well preserved as fossils.

(iv) The exine is not continuous because it has prominent apertures called **germ pores**, where sporopollenin is absent. During germination the **pollen tube emerges through a germ pore**, so the outermost layer has to be interrupted at these places.
